results.message: Was Augustine's account of Pelagius fair?

voice_event.speaker: lpc
voice_event.text:
We cannot say whether Augustine's account of Pelagius is fair, because we do not have Pelagius's own voice to set beside it. What reaches us is Augustine's side of the dispute, argued at length across thirteen works. He refused a claim he set out as the Pelagian one: that a believer's own moral effort is enough without grace. Whether Pelagius himself held it in that form is contested. The word grace occurs 1,798 times in those thirteen works alone. That is real teaching, argued in earnest. But it is one voice, in one body of work, prompted by a live dispute.

The conviction itself is ours. A heading in Cyprian's handbook of proof texts says we must boast in nothing, since nothing is our own: “We must boast in nothing, since nothing is our own. The Gospel according to John says, ‘No one can receive anything unless it is given to him from heaven.’ Paul's first letter to the Corinthians also says, ‘What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?’”

Augustine quoted those very words against the Pelagians. But whether he fairly represents the man he argued against, we cannot say from inside our own record. What we have is what Augustine taught, not what Pelagius answered.

glosses.plain_meaning: For us, grace is the insistence that no effort of ours is enough on its own. Any good a person does was given to them before they did it.
glosses.quick_meaning: For us, grace means this: no one's own effort is ever enough. Whatever good a person does was given to them first.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern listener is likely to hear grace as a warm general benevolence, or as 'grace under pressure,' or as a denominational shibboleth they may already have an opinion about, and to hear our anti-Pelagian position as harsh determinism. We mean a specific and contested claim about the priority of divine action over human capacity, argued against a named opponent over roughly a decade, with direct consequences for how a congregation is taught, how failure is handled, and what a pastor can reasonably ask of anyone.
false_friend: a warm general benevolence, or 'grace under pressure,' with no specific claim about the priority of divine action over human capacity
a denominational shibboleth in a Protestant-Catholic argument the participant may already hold an opinion about

names.name: Augustinius of Hippo Regius, presbyter 391, bishop 395/396-430

figures_used.bridge_line: Our bishop at Hippo. The people seized him and brought him to be made a presbyter while he wept. Later they pressed him into the bishop's office over his own refusal. He spent his last days weeping over psalms of penitence, while an army lay outside the walls.

dates.display: converted 386, baptised 387; seized by the congregation at Hippo and ordained presbyter against his own wishes in 391, weeping through it (Possidius, Vita IV); designated coadjutor and consecrated bishop of Hippo by Megalius, primate of Numidia, in 395/396, again amid popular acclamation (Possidius, Vita VIII); died 430, during the Vandal siege of Hippo

names.name: Thascius Caecilius Cyprianus, bishop of Carthage (248/249-258)

figures_used.bridge_line: Our bishop, chosen while still new to the faith, over his own reluctance. During a plague he taught us to love even our enemies. He was put to death under Valerian.

dates.display: a trained rhetorician who turned from a public career to Christian life, converted c. 246; ordained and elected bishop of Carthage between roughly July 248 and April 249 by the acclamation of the Carthaginian people, over the recorded opposition of five presbyters, while still newly baptised, as his deacon Pontius tells it; banished to Curubis under the Valerianic persecution; executed under the emperor Valerian in 258

confidence.divergence_note: The entire evidentiary base for this term is one voice (Augustine) within one evidence stream (the anti-Pelagian corpus), flagged at generation rather than discovered afterwards (Author-Gravity-Risk: Yes). No Pelagian first-person answer survives in our own record. This term also carries a live scholarly contest, kept on its own axis, independent of this historical-fact rating. The contest type is Relationship to present-day traditions, secondarily Meaning. It runs over how the historical position stands to the way living traditions use the word now, including later appropriations and the Catholic-Protestant disagreements that ran through them, and over the modern reassessment of whether the position Augustine argued against is the one Pelagius held. The entry does not present the anti-Pelagian position as the settled meaning of the word across Christian history, and it does not characterize Pelagius.

The text field is the ANF English as printed. The source gives the two proof texts with bare labels ('In the Gospel according to John:'); modern_rendering adds the verb 'says' to each so that it reads as a sentence. The Latin heading is In nullo gloriandum, quando nostrum nihil sit.
